read.sections.0.text.source: Around 1900, more people began to use cars and electricity. Car tyres were made with rubber, and electric wires needed a rubber cover to keep them safe. So people wanted much more rubber. In British Malaya and Singapore, land was cleared and rubber trees were planted. A rubber tree gives a milky liquid called latex. A worker tapped each tree by cutting a thin line in its bark, carefully, so the tree was not harmed. Then workers collected the latex, and others made it into flat sheets that could be shipped. Rubber grew on large estates and on small farms too.
read.sections.0.text.back: Around 1900, more and more people began to use cars and electricity. Car tyres were made with rubber, and electric cables needed a rubber wrapping to be safe. So people wanted much more rubber. In British Malaya and Singapore, land was cleared and rubber trees were planted. A rubber tree produces a milk-like liquid called latex. A worker tapped each tree by scoring a thin line in the bark of its trunk, carefully, so the tree was not damaged. Then workers collected the latex, and other workers processed it into flat sheets that could be sent by ship. Rubber grew on large estates and also on small gardens.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Tapped each tree by cutting a thin line in its bark" → "menyadap … dengan menggores garis tipis di kulit batangnya". "Menyadap" is the usual Indonesian word for tapping rubber; "small farms" → "kebun-kebun kecil" (smallholdings, "kebun rakyat").

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Around 1900, people began to use cars and electricity. Car tyres needed rubber. Electric wires needed a rubber cover. So people wanted lots of rubber. In Malaya and Singapore, people planted rubber trees. A rubber tree gives a white liquid called latex. A worker cuts a thin line in the tree. Workers collect the latex. Then it is made into sheets and sent away. Rubber grew on big estates and on small farms.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Around 1900, people began to use cars and electricity. Car tyres needed rubber. Electric cables needed a rubber wrapping. So people wanted a lot of rubber. In Malaya and Singapore, people planted rubber trees. A rubber tree produces a white liquid called latex. A worker scores a thin line in the tree. Workers collect the latex. Then the latex is made into sheets and sent somewhere else. Rubber grew on big estates and on small gardens.

read.sections.1.text.source: Rubber could bring big profits, but starting an estate cost a lot of money. In 1898, a merchant called Tan Chay Yan started Asahan Estate in Melaka, one of the first in Malaya. Later, an investor in London could buy shares in a company that owned estates. Many workers came from South India. Some came under indenture, a contract that tied a worker to one employer for several years. Many indentured workers had debts, and their pay was lower than that of free workers. Indenture ended in 1910. Under the kangany system, an overseer recruited workers, and more families came. Some people came freely. These systems help explain why a worker's choices were not the same as an owner's.
read.sections.1.text.back: Rubber could bring big profits, but opening an estate needed a lot of money. In 1898, a merchant named Tan Chay Yan opened Asahan Estate in Melaka, one of the first in Malaya. Later, an investor in London could buy shares in a company that owned estates. Many workers came from South India. Some came under a bound contract, that is, a contract that tied a worker to one employer for several years. Many workers bound by contract had debts, and their wages were lower than free workers' wages. Bound contracts ended in 1910. In the kangany system, a foreman recruited workers, and more families came. Some people came freely. These systems help explain why a worker's choices were not the same as an owner's choices.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Rubber could make owners rich. In 1898, a merchant called Tan Chay Yan started a rubber estate. Later, an investor in London could pay money into rubber companies. Many workers came from South India. Some came under indenture. This contract tied them to one boss for years. Many had debts and low pay. Indenture ended in 1910. In the kangany system, a boss found workers. More families came this way. Some people came freely.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Rubber could make the owners rich. In 1898, a merchant named Tan Chay Yan opened a rubber estate. Later, an investor in London could put money into rubber companies. Many workers came from South India. Some came under a bound contract. This contract tied them to one boss for years. Many had debts and low wages. Bound contracts ended in 1910. In the kangany system, a foreman found workers. More families came this way. Some people came freely.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: "Pay money into" → "menanamkan uang" (invest), which links to the glossary's definition of investor.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo printed in 1914 in a souvenir book about Singapore. A Singapore hotel published the book as a souvenir. The photo shows rows of rubber trees and a worker at a tree with a bucket. The book's makers chose this scene to show visitors. The photo cannot tell us the workers' names or pay. It cannot tell us how they came, or whether they were free to leave. For those questions, we need other sources, such as pay records, contracts or a worker's own account. One photo from Singapore also cannot stand for every estate in Malaya.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo printed in 1914 in a souvenir book about Singapore. A hotel in Singapore published the book as a souvenir. The photo shows rows of rubber trees and a worker at a tree with a bucket. The book's makers chose this scene to show visitors. The photo cannot tell us the workers' names or wages. The photo cannot tell us how they came, or whether they were free to leave. For those questions, we need other sources, such as wage records, contracts or a worker's own story. One photo from Singapore also cannot stand for every estate in Malaya.

For that, we need other sources, like wage records or the words of the workers.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Indenture and kangany recruitment meant debt, hard work and low pay for many workers; the National Library article says critics called indenture “near slavery” and said kangany recruiters misled some people. Keep both truths: don't call every migrant enslaved, and don't call every arrangement free. Some learners may have moved for work, or know people who did: never ask learners about their own or their family's journeys, work, pay, legal status, home country, religion or ethnicity. There is no worker's own account in this lesson, and none should be invented; when learners imagine a worker, they write questions to investigate, not a made-up life story.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Bound contracts and recruitment through the kangany meant debt, hard work and low wages for many workers; the National Library article says critics called bound contracts “almost like slavery” and said kangany recruiters deceived some people. Hold on to both truths: do not call every migrant enslaved, and do not call every arrangement free. Some learners may have moved for work, or know people who have: never ask learners about their own or their family's journeys, work, wages, legal status, home country, religion or ethnicity. There is no worker's own story in this lesson, and none may be made up; when learners imagine a worker, they write questions to investigate, not a made-up life story.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners back one benefit and one worker constraint with a source, and say what the 1914 photo cannot show. Evidence move (brief 3B): pair the investor record (Source 1) with the recruitment history (Source 2), then look at the 1914 souvenir photo. A sound answer gives a benefit and a constraint backed by sources, not guessed from the picture. Misconceptions to catch: not every Indian migrant was a rubber tapper (many were merchants, clerks or teachers), not every tapper was indentured, ownership was not only British (Tan Chay Yan and other Chinese merchants owned estates, and small farmers grew rubber), and one Singapore photo cannot stand for every estate in Malaya.
educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners support one benefit and one constraint for workers with a source, and say what the 1914 photo cannot show. Step for reading the evidence (brief 3B): pair the record about investors (Source 1) with the history of recruitment (Source 2), then look at the 1914 souvenir photo. A good answer gives one benefit and one constraint supported by sources, not guessed from the picture. Misunderstandings to watch for: not every Indian migrant was a rubber tapper (many were traders, clerks or teachers), not every tapper was bound by contract, ownership was not only in British hands (Tan Chay Yan and other Chinese merchants owned estates, and smallholders grew rubber), and one photo from Singapore cannot stand for every estate in Malaya.

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: both National Library articles are modern histories, not workers' records. The 12,000 acres belonged to one group of London companies, not to all rubber land. The 1914 book was made by a hotel for its guests. The National Heritage Board's record for a similar postcard says indenture tied workers to a three-year contract; the National Library article says five years at first, cut to three in 1872, so the lesson says “several years”.
educatorNotes.1.back: Note about sources: both National Library articles are histories from today, not workers' records. The 12,000 acres belonged to one group of London companies, not all rubber land. The 1914 book was made by a hotel for its guests. The National Heritage Board's record for a similar postcard says the bound contract tied workers to a three-year contract; the National Library article says five years at first, cut to three years in 1872, so this lesson says “several years”.
